Black
BLAK
a.
From Anglo-Saxon blaec, dark, of the darkest colour. Webster 1828: of the colour of night; destitute of light; dark. Scripture uses it of skin without disparagement, of a horse of famine, and of heavens that mourn.

Biblical Definition

The Song of Solomon opens with a woman describing herself without apology and without shame: I am black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, as the tents of Kedar, as the curtains of Solomon (Song of Solomon 1:5), the next verse explaining that the sun had looked upon her because her brothers had made her keeper of the vineyards. Job uses the word of a body wrecked by disease: My skin is black upon me, and my bones are burned with heat (Job 30:30). In Revelation the third seal brings a black horse whose rider carries a balance, and the voice that follows prices wheat and barley at a day’s wage for a day’s food: I beheld, and lo a black horse; and he that sat on him had a pair of balances in his hand (Revelation 6:5). Our Lord uses the colour to prove how little a man governs: Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black (Matthew 5:36) — the argument against oaths is that the swearer has nothing of his own to pledge.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BLACK as of the colour of night; destitute of light; dark; and figuratively, dismal, gloomy, sullen, or wicked.

expand to see more

BLACK, a. — Of the colour of night; destitute of light; dark.

Dark; dismal; gloomy; sullen; as a black day.

Sullenly angry; as a black look.

BLACK, n. — That which is destitute of light or whiteness; the darkest colour.

Anglo-Saxon blaec, black; distinguish the related blac, pale or shining.

Key Scripture

Song of Solomon 1:5 — "I am black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, as the tents of Kedar, as the curtains of Solomon."

Job 30:30 — "My skin is black upon me, and my bones are burned with heat."

Revelation 6:5 — "And when he had opened the third seal, I heard the third beast say, Come and see. And I beheld, and lo a black horse; and he that sat on him had a pair of balances in his hand."

Matthew 5:36 — "Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black."

Modern Corruption

Scripture’s use of black for skin carries no disparagement whatever, and the attempt to enlist the Bible for racial hierarchy has always required doing violence to its plain text.

expand to see more

The bride of the Song says I am black, but comely, and the following verse gives the cause — the sun had looked upon her because she had been set to keep vineyards. The text records a fact about complexion and immediately calls her beautiful; there is no hierarchy in it. The Bible’s anthropology forecloses any such hierarchy at the root: all men are of one blood (Acts 17:26), all descend from one Adam and share original sin (Romans 5:12), and all who are in Christ are one (Galatians 3:28). The so-called curse of Ham, long misused to justify slavery, is not in the text at all — Genesis 9:25 curses Canaan, not Ham, and concerns a people in the land, not a race. The dictionary names that misreading as the corruption it is.

Having said that, the biblical answer to racial hierarchy is not the modern framework that replaces it. Critical race theory and the antiracist frameworks built on it substitute an oppressor-oppressed binary based on race for the biblical categories of sin, the fallen heart, and covenant. That is a competing anthropology, not a development of the Christian one, and it cannot deliver what it promises because it has no doctrine of forgiveness and no category for a guilt that is actually removed. Scripture’s account is more radical in both directions: every man is guilty in Adam, and every man in Christ is one new man. Revelation 7:9 shows the outcome — a great multitude of all nations and kindreds and people and tongues before the throne.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shachor (H7838), black; shachar (H7835), to be black or dusky; Greek melas (G3189), black; the root of English melancholy and melanin.

expand to see more

Hebrew shachor (H7838) — black, dusky; I am black, but comely (Song of Solomon 1:5).

Hebrew shachar (H7835) — to be black or grow dark; my skin is black upon me (Job 30:30).

Greek melas (G3189) — black; the third horse of Revelation 6:5 and the hair of Matthew 5:36.

Hebrew Qedar (H6938) — Kedar, whose tents were of dark goats’ hair; the bride’s comparison.

Greek zugos (G2218) — a yoke or balance; carried by the rider of the black horse, a symbol of scarcity.

Usage

"I am black, but comely (Song of Solomon 1:5) — a fact of complexion, and beauty affirmed in the same breath."

"Lo a black horse; and he that sat on him had a pair of balances (Revelation 6:5) — famine, rationed by weight."

"Thou canst not make one hair white or black (Matthew 5:36) — the swearer has nothing of his own to pledge."
